The festival entertainment at Central College came in according to programme last FRIDAY night. As soon as the announcement was made public that there would be entertainment at the College, the pleasure seeking portion of our people felt sure of all opportunity of spending a pleasant evening. But when they knew that it WAS to be the festival entertainment, under the care of the ladies of the school, assisted by the ladies of the Methodist church, everyone knew there was a u-u in store for those who should attend. The night WAS rather dark and cold, and the roads out of town were amply horrible. So that no one from the country could attend, and we know there would have been quite a number from the country had the roads been good. However, there WAS about as large a crowd present as the building could comfortably contain. The two large halls were continually full of prominence. The parlors and cloak rooms were full, and ladies and gentlemen were to be seen everywhere. The large dining room was crowded all the time, there being no vacant space at the tables, and scarce standing room anywhere. Such a crowd of beautiful ladies is seldom seen in Lexington, and never seen anywhere else. A large number of gallant young gentlemen were present. Of course, and as the ladies were numerous, sociable and pretty, the gentlemen enjoyed the evenings.

THE DANCING HALL

presented all animated and attractive appearances. Aside from the large number of beautiful ladies present, who would have made any room attractive, there was a fine display of fruit and flowers, and the tables were crowded with large and handsome cakes. The most delicate taste could not find fault with the display of good things which were there to tempt the appetite. On the wall immediately in front of the entrance, was a canvas containing, in large letters, "WELCOME." In the southeast corner of the room stood

REFRESHMENT TABLE No. 1.

under the care of Mrs. Winsor, Mrs. Robert Taubman, Miss Laura Paynes, Miss Nettie Winsor, Miss Fannie Porter and Miss Kate Graham. We have not space to give a minute description of the tables. The stand dealt in ice cream, cakes, candy, &c., and presented very handsome appearance. The cake was large, pretty and good, and the cream was all that could be desired. The receipts were $5. In the northeast corner of the room was

REFRESHMENT TABLE No. 2.

kept by Mrs. Chas. Alistair, Miss Ruby Davis, Mrs. Lizzie Crowder and Miss Anna Hays. There was also a beautifully decorated table. Ice cream, cake, candy, &c. Both tables, however, were well patronized, but there was a lack of suitable tables in parties wishing to sit down and enjoy refreshments; it was, perhaps, a mistake to allow any tables in the room without them; without them, every guest would have been forced to stand. We are certain that much more cream would have been sold had there been more tables, or none at all. It was a mistake was made in favor of the comfort of the people in the receipts at table number TWO were $8. In the north side of the room was

THE POST OFFICE.

which was under the care of Miss Susie Dixie and Miss Lillie Grissom. The office was run in the first-class STYLE, and when anyone went there for a letter he was sure to get it. We rather LIKE that kind of post office, even if the ordinary POSTAL rules were reversed, and letters sent on credit, but received for cash. The getting of LETTERS, and such sweet ones, overbalances all drawbacks. The receipts were $5. In the center of the room stood

THE FRUIT TABLE.

which was under the charge of Mrs. Winsor, Mrs. H. Macy, Miss Kramer and Miss Alice Fletcher. This stand was quite pretty, the orange tree being something new. Its crop of orange SEEMED inexhaustible. The stand was grapes, which were very tempting, and sold readily. A wreath of pretty flowers ran entirely around it, as shown by the receipts, which were $5. In the west end of the room were the

OYSTER AND MAT TABLES.

presided over by Mrs. Susan Bar, Mrs. Jacob Price, Miss Emma Addison and Miss F. Potter. These ladies were kept very busy waiting on their numerous patrons. They kept two tables—one where they served a regular supper, and the other where they served fresh oysters. Their oysters were excellent, and the coffee was what it should have been. The receipts at this table were $40.

BOUQUETS.

A bouquet was voted to the prettiest girl; Miss Eddie Winsor received 15 votes and the bouquet. There were many other votes cast for different young ladies, and the bouquet brought $2.20 into the treasury. Other flowers were sold for smaller sums, bringing the sum up to $40.

RECAPITULATIONS

The receipts at the door were $31. From other sources, not named above, $30. The total receipts from all sources, were $187.45; total expenses, $65; leaving a balance of $122.45 as the net results of the entertainment, which, in these hard times, is doing remarkably well.
